If the revised pay is within 10%, the offer letter gets prepared and sent. If it's still over 10%, it goes back to the director again.

The first counter goes back to comp review and is subject to the same 10% and director rules, and then a revised offer is sent. When the employee counters that second time, it counts as a decline, so both managers get notified and the ticket is closed with no further offer.

answer.explanation: When a user asks for an MFA reset, the desk opens a ticket, looks up the user in the directory, and calls them back only on the number on file, ignoring any different number they offer, since phone resets are a common way attackers get into accounts. If the person answers, they must correctly give their employee ID and manager's name, and if either fails or they say they never asked, the case goes to Security Operations and nothing gets reset. For a passing user, the analyst checks group membership, and privileged accounts need IAM on-call approval before going further. The reset itself clears old MFA registrations, issues a temporary access pass good for 8 hours that gets read to the user, and sends the MFA reset email to both the user and their manager so anyone who did not request it will notice, then the ticket is marked Resolved.

answer.explanation: When someone calls to say they lost their authenticator, the help desk doesn't act on the request right away. First it gets logged in a ticket with the caller's name, the username, and a callback number. The user's real mobile number comes from the company directory, and the desk only uses that number, even if the caller asks for a different one because they're traveling or got a new phone. The desk hangs up and calls the directory number. If nobody picks up, they leave a generic voicemail asking the person to call the help desk about the ticket, wait half an hour, and try once more before closing the ticket as unable to verify. Once someone answers, they have to pass two checks, the employee ID and the manager's name. If the check fails or the person says they never asked for a reset, the desk stops, changes nothing, and passes the ticket to Security Operations as possible social engineering. If the checks pass, the desk looks at group membership. Privileged accounts need an IAM approval before anything changes. answer.explanation: Each morning before first wave, the covering person pulls the day's list of about 40 bins from the WMS, puts a count hold on all of them so pickers don't touch them, and counts each bin blind in eaches. The system compares the count to on-hand. If the difference is small enough (under 2% and under $50), it posts automatically and the hold comes off. If not, a different person recounts without seeing the first number. If the recount agrees with the system, the first count was just a mistake and gets logged as a count error. If the recount agrees with the first count, the variance is real, so the cause gets researched: unconfirmed picks, unconfirmed putaways, received ASNs not yet put away, and the adjacent bins. If the cause is found, the transaction gets fixed directly. If not, an adjustment goes to the shift supervisor for sign-off. If the recount matches neither number, Dana does a third count and that becomes the recount to run through the same check. Holds that sit too long and are hurting waves can be pulled early by the supervisor, and the bin gets counted again the next day.
trace_answers: The first count is out of tolerance and the recount matches the first count, so the variance is treated as real. Research finds a putaway that was never confirmed, so I confirm that putaway in the WMS. No adjustment is needed. Then I release the hold and log the bin in the tracker with the cause code for an unconfirmed putaway.

The recount matches neither the first count nor the system, so Dana does a third count. Dana's count matches the first count, so it is treated as the recount and the variance is real. Research turns up no cause, so I key an adjustment request and send it to the shift supervisor. Once the supervisor approves it in the WMS and it posts, I release the hold and log the bin in the tracker as unexplained.

All three key decisions are framed as choice points with correct branch outcomes. Both edge cases are covered: Dana's third count loops back through the recount check, and the supervisor's early hold kill re-queues the bin for the next day. Both traces are correct, and nothing contradicts the source; the only small blemish is that the 'matches neither' branch is listed at the end of the stage sequence rather than with the recount comparison.

answer.explanation: This is the process for handling a leave of absence request that comes into the HR leave inbox. The request gets logged in the case tracker first so the timing starts, then the employee's tenure is checked in the HRIS. People with less than a year get forwarded to Okafor, who decides whether to approve unprotected leave, and nobody on the queue denies those requests directly. Medical leave triggers a certification form, and the certification has to be signed and show dates and expected duration; incomplete ones go back for correction, but if 15 calendar days pass without a complete one, a provisional denial goes out and the case is flagged up. Once cleared, the manager only gets the start and end dates, never the medical details. Then the leave is entered in the HRIS with the right code, payroll is contacted first if the leave runs past 30 days, and the approval letter goes to the employee. A return check-in is booked for the week before the end date. Extensions restart the certification cycle if requested before the end, and go to Okafor if requested after. When the person comes back, medical leave needs a fitness-for-duty clearance, and restricted clearances go to the HR business partner before reactivation, while personal leave just gets reactivated and closed.
trace_answers: An employee with 8 months of service is under the 12-month threshold, so the request goes to Okafor for a discretionary decision. Since she approved it, the case carries on as a normal case with 'unprotected' ticked in the tracker. Because the leave is medical, the certification form goes out to the employee. The complete certification comes back on the second try, inside the 15-day window, so it passes review. The manager gets only the 45-day start and end dates. The leave is then entered in the HRIS with the medical leave code. Since 45 days is over 30, payroll is emailed the dates so they can set up direct billing for benefit premiums before the approval letter goes to the employee. A return-to-work check-in gets put on the calendar for the week before the end date.

An employee with 3 years of service is eligible for protected leave, so there is no tenure issue. Because the leave was medical, the employee has to bring back a fitness-for-duty clearance from their provider. Since the clearance has restrictions, it doesn't go straight back to HRIS. It gets handed to the HR business partner for an accommodation review, and the employee is only reactivated once the HR business partner says to go ahead. After reactivation, the case is closed.

The certification timeout and both extension paths are fully covered. The manager-confidentiality edge case is only partly covered: the student says the manager never gets medical details but omits referring the manager to the HR lead or Okafor. Both trace answers match the key.

answer.explanation: When someone wants to stop a personal check, the teller or phone rep first confirms who they are and that they have authority over the account. answer.explanation: Mobile deposit exceptions are worked from a queue, always starting with the oldest item, because anything not dispositioned by the 6pm ET cutoff rolls to the next business day and delays the customer's funds. Each item is first screened for date validity, with a stricter 6-month limit for most checks and a 1-year allowance for Treasury checks. Next the images are checked for legibility and the required endorsement and signature. Failures get a retake-photos rejection, and repeated failures on the same check escalate to a branch visit with a block on that check number. The written amount is then compared with the keyed amount; small differences under $25 are corrected to the written figure, while larger ones are rejected for resubmission. Items that pass go through a duplicate search, and if the account has a repeat duplicate within 90 days the case is referred to Fraud Ops instead of sending the customer a standard rejection. Clean items get a hold assigned, extended for new accounts or amounts over $5,000 and standard otherwise, and are then accepted so they post. Every disposition and reason code is logged in the tracker so resubmissions can be counted.

The item is not corrected by hand. Because it stops at the amount check, the account being two weeks old never comes into play, no hold is set, and the disposition and R2 code are logged in the tracker.

The item clears the date, image, and amount checks, then the duplicate search hits. Since the same account had another duplicate hit 60 days ago, which is within 90 days, the item goes to Fraud Ops through the referral form. The customer does not get the R3 email, no hold is applied, the item is not accepted, and the referral is still logged in the tracker.

answer.explanation: A student begins by submitting a Learning Agreement, and the eligibility check requires a 2.5 GPA and 60 earned credits, with a department chair petition available as a fallback. The employer must then be confirmed: companies already on the Approved Sites list go straight to the supervisor, while new companies first pass a vetting call and get added to the list. The Site Verification form is sent to the supervisor, who has 10 business days to return it, with one reminder and a further 5 business days before the application is placed on hold for an alternate contact. Once the form is back, the faculty sponsor reviews the learning objectives, with up to two revision rounds before an in-person meeting is required. The student is then registered, using a Late Add form with registrar signature if add/drop has passed. If the supervisor never returns the verification form, the process first sends one reminder after the initial 10 business days. answer.explanation: A cashier's check at this bank is only issued to someone who already banks here and is an owner on the account being charged, or an authorized signer on a business account per the signer card. The payee name has to be taken exactly as the customer wants it, read back to them, and the remitter defaults to the account holder and cannot be someone else. The amount plus the $10 fee must fit within the available balance, not the ledger balance, and if it does not, the customer can move money from another account they have with the bank, or lower the amount, but a check is never issued for more than the funds allow. Premier accounts usually skip the fee, though the product code should be double checked. Anything above $10,000 needs a supervisor to enter an override before the check will print, and the supervisor also countersigns it. The account is debited and the check printed on official stock from the locked drawer. If the check has a printing error after printing, it cannot be given out; it gets voided, logged, filed, and reprinted, and the reprint does not add another fee. Once it is correct, the customer checks it, the teller signs it, and the customer gets the check with a receipt while the bank copy goes in the end of day batch.

The account is debited $12,500, the check is printed on official stock, the customer reviews payee and amount, the teller signs, the supervisor countersigns, and then the customer gets the check and receipt while the bank copy goes in the batch envelope.

Standard checking customer requesting $4,000 with $3,500 available: the $10 fee applies, so $4,010 is needed and $510 is short. Because the customer has $6,000 in savings with the bank, an internal transfer of at least $510 is done from savings, then available balance is rechecked. Since the amount is under $10,000, no override is needed. The account is debited $4,010, the check is printed, reviewed, signed, and handed over with the receipt, and the bank copy goes in the batch envelope.

answer.explanation: Requests arrive in the FW-Changes queue, oldest first unless one is tagged emergency. Each one is first checked for a complete form, and incomplete ones go back to the requester, who has five business days to reply before the ticket is abandoned automatically. Blank expiry dates get a 90-day default, and any/any requests are rejected right away without scoring. External destinations are checked against the threat intel blocklist, and anything listed gets rejected with a note to the SOC. Everything else gets scored on the risk sheet. Scores under 7 can be approved by the team, while 7 or higher goes to the security architect, who can approve, deny, or send it back for changes. Approved requests are scheduled for the next Tuesday or Thursday night window, unless they are manager-approved emergencies, which go in immediately. On the night, the rule is staged and pushed, then tested with the requester on a call. A failed test means rolling back, fixing, and retrying once, and a second failure escalates the ticket to the network engineering lead without closing it. A passing test means the rule gets tagged with the ticket number and expiry date, and the ticket is closed. Emergency changes also need a retroactive CAB record within 24 hours, and the rule is pulled if CAB rejects it.
trace_answers: The request is scored 8, so it goes to the architect, who approves it. It is scheduled for the next Tuesday or Thursday change window. On the night, the rule is pushed and the connectivity test fails, so the rule is rolled back and the network team is consulted. After a fix, the retry also fails, so the rule is rolled back again, the ticket is marked Failed Implementation, it is escalated to the network engineering lead, the requester is told it is escalated, and the ticket stays open.

The emergency is manager-approved and internal, so it skips the change window and is implemented right away. It scores 4, so no architect review is needed. The connectivity test passes, so the rule is tagged with the ticket number and expiry date, the requester is notified, and the ticket is closed. Because it was an emergency, a retroactive CAB record was filed. When CAB rejects it, the rule is pulled.

Minor deductions apply for imposing a strict linear order on the expiry and any/any checks that the workflow does not specify, and for omitting the 24-hour CAB deadline in trace 2. Both traces are otherwise correct.

answer.explanation: Refill requests come in by portal or phone and get logged in the queue with the key patient and medication details. The first real check is how long it has been since the patient was last seen by a provider. If that visit was within the last year, the request goes right to the nurse pool. If it was longer ago, the request does not go to nursing yet; the patient gets a call to book a follow-up, and the clinic can authorize a single 30-day bridge supply so they are not without medication before that visit, which then goes through the nurse pool like any other refill. In the nurse pool, an RN compares the medication against the refill protocol. Routine medications on protocol are approved and sent to the pharmacy by the RN. Controlled substances and anything off protocol go to the prescribing provider, who either approves and sends it or denies it. Provider inbox items are expected to be handled within 2 business days, and if one sits longer, the RN escalates it to whoever is covering that day. Once the request is sent or denied, the patient is told the outcome and the request is closed in the queue.
trace_answers: a. The patient was last seen 18 months ago, so the request cannot go straight to nursing. The clinic calls the patient to book a follow-up appointment and authorizes one 30-day bridge supply. That bridge refill then goes to the nurse pool, where the RN checks the blood pressure medication against protocol. Since it is a routine on-protocol medication, the RN approves it and e-sends it to the pharmacy. The patient is notified of the outcome and the request is closed.

b. The patient was seen 3 months ago, so the request goes to the nurse pool. Because it is a controlled substance, the RN routes it to the prescribing provider's inbox rather than approving it. The provider is out for a week, so the item sits unactioned. After 2 business days, the RN escalates it to the covering provider for that day, who approves or denies it. If approved, the covering provider e-sends it to the pharmacy. The patient is notified and the request is closed.

Both trace answers match the key.

answer.explanation: A leave of absence request starts when the form lands in the HR leave inbox and gets logged in the case tracker so the clock begins. The employee's service is then checked in the HRIS. Anyone with under 12 months is not automatically denied; the request goes to the HR manager, R. Okafor, who decides whether to grant discretionary unprotected leave, and if she says no the employee gets the denial letter and the case closes. Medical leave triggers a certification form, which must come back signed by the provider with dates and expected duration; incomplete certifications are sent back with the missing items listed, and if no complete one arrives within 15 calendar days of the form first going out, a provisional denial goes out and the HR manager is flagged. Once certification clears, or for personal leave where it is skipped, the manager gets only the start and end dates, never the certification or diagnosis. The leave is then entered in the HRIS with the right code, payroll is emailed for direct billing of premiums if the leave runs over 30 days, the approval letter goes to the employee, and a return-to-work check-in is booked for the week before the end date. Extensions are handled as a fresh certification cycle before the end date and go to Okafor if requested after it. On return, medical cases need a fitness-for-duty clearance; a full clearance means reactivation and closing, while restrictions mean an accommodation review with the HR business partner before reactivation. Personal leave just gets reactivated and closed.
trace_answers: An employee with 8 months of service is under the 12-month threshold, so the request is forwarded to R. Okafor, who approves it as discretionary unprotected leave, and the case is ticked unprotected in the tracker. Because it is medical, the certification form goes out. The complete certification comes back on the second attempt within the 15-day window, so it is checked for provider signature, dates, and expected duration, and since it passes, the manager is emailed only the start and end dates. The leave is entered in the HRIS with the correct medical code. Because 45 days is over 30, payroll is emailed the dates so they can set up direct billing for benefit premiums, then the approval letter goes to the employee and a return-to-work check-in is put on the calendar for the week before the end date.

A medical leave employee with 3 years of service is eligible for protected leave, so there is no unprotected step. On return, the fitness-for-duty clearance from the provider is collected. Because it has restrictions rather than being a full clearance, the case goes to the HR business partner for an accommodation review. The employee is not reactivated in the HRIS yet, and reactivation only happens when the HR business partner says to proceed, after which the case can be closed.

answer.explanation: This process handles equipment setup for new hires. answer.explanation: When an account holder dies, the bank first needs a certified death certificate and government ID from whoever is reporting it. Until those arrive, the profile only gets a soft flag and nothing is frozen or closed. Once they are in, every account the deceased owned gets a hard freeze that day, and cards are cancelled while autopays and scheduled transfers are stopped. Next, the transaction history from the date of death forward is checked for federal benefit payments such as Social Security or VA deposits. Any of those get sent back to Treasury and that amount is held. After that, the account type decides the path. Joint accounts with survivorship just get retitled to the survivor and the freeze is lifted, so they never go to legal. Sole-owner accounts are checked for a POD beneficiary, who can claim with ID, a death certificate copy, and supervisor sign-off without legal review. If there is no POD, the balance after the hold determines whether a small estate affidavit or court letters are needed, and then the package goes to Legal Review. A rejected package goes back to the family to fix, but a second rejection goes to the Estate Services Manager. Approved payouts are made by cashier's check in the right name, and then the account is closed and the closure letter with final interest is mailed. If the family goes silent for 90 days after a document request, the file goes to the Dormant Estate queue and the account stays frozen.
trace_answers: A sole-owner account with no POD and a $41,000 balance needs letters testamentary or letters of administration naming the executor, since the balance is over $25,000. The package goes to Legal Review. If legal rejects it the first time, the family gets the reasons and resubmits. When legal rejects the same file a second time, the file is escalated to the Estate Services Manager, who takes it over from there and the back and forth stops.

A sole-owner account with a POD beneficiary that received a Social Security deposit after the date of death first gets a Treasury reclamation submitted for that deposit with the amount held. Then the beneficiary brings their ID and a copy of the death certificate, and the branch ops supervisor signs off on the claim form. Legal review is not needed for POD claims, so the payout goes out as a cashier's check to the beneficiary and the account is closed.

answer.explanation: This process handles relocation stipend requests for interns. Requests are first screened by distance from home to the site, and anyone under 50 miles or fully remote receives a not-eligible notice and is closed out. Eligible requests have their lease and first-payment proof checked, and any gaps are returned to the intern for correction, with the request closed as Incomplete if no fix arrives within five business days. Once documents are accepted, the amount is set at a standard 1500 dollars unless a higher amount is requested, in which case the hiring manager signs first and Finance reviews it, with the standard amount used if Finance declines. The manager must approve the request, with escalation to the department head after three business days without a response, and a rejection ends the request with an email to the intern. After approval, the intern must sign the repayment agreement before anything goes to payroll, and submissions made before Wednesday noon are paid that Friday. Finally, the intern receives a confirmation email with the amount and pay date, and the tracker is marked Paid/Scheduled.

The amount drops back to the standard 1500 dollars without contacting the intern, the process continues to the repayment agreement and payroll, and the confirmation email notes that Finance capped the amount.

For an eligible intern whose lease is unsigned, the request is returned with a note asking for the signed lease. If the intern does not re-upload within 5 business days, the request is closed as Incomplete in the tracker. The intern may submit one fresh resubmission, which starts over at the distance check.

answer.explanation: Hardship applications are pulled from the queue oldest first unless flagged urgent, and every application starts with an enrollment check, since students who are not at least half-time this term are denied straight away with the appeal information and off-campus resource link. Eligible students are then checked in the fund tracker for any award earlier in the academic year, and a prior award sends the case to the Dean of Students director no matter the amount, with the prior total placed at the top of the summary and the yearly cap of 1,500 limiting what can be approved. Missing documents trigger an email with a 5 business day window, one reminder with 3 more business days, and closure as incomplete if nothing arrives, though a student can reapply at any time and starts over. Once docs are complete, the case summary is written and small requests of 750 or less with no prior award can be approved by the coordinator, while larger ones go to the Tuesday committee, which can approve in full, approve a partial amount, or deny. Any approved amount is sent to Financial Aid for a cost of attendance check before the student is told, and the amount is cut to the cap Financial Aid gives if needed. The award email goes out next, then the Bursar disbursement form, where a balance is paid first unless the case is tagged housing or food, in which case the direct to student box is checked and the full amount goes to the student. Every case ends by logging the outcome and amount in the tracker and closing it in the portal. Urgent eviction or shutoff cases get up to 300 approved the same day before documents arrive.

The case summary is written once docs are complete, and the committee approves a partial 800. The 800 goes to Financial Aid first, and after they clear it the award email is sent to the student. Since the student owes a balance and the application is not tagged housing or food, the Bursar applies the grant to the balance first and any remainder goes to the student by direct deposit. The outcome and amount are logged in the fund tracker and the case is closed in the portal.

The prior award of 1,000 means the Dean of Students director must sign off no matter the amount, and the 1,000 goes at the top of the summary. With 1,500 as the yearly cap, only 500 remains, so the director can approve at most 500 of the 700 requested and the rest cannot be granted now. The approved amount goes to Financial Aid for the cost of attendance check, then the award email goes out, and the Bursar disbursement form is filled out with the direct to student box checked because this is a housing emergency. That means the Bursar skips the balance and deposits the full approved amount to the student. The result is logged in the fund tracker and the case is closed in the portal.

answer.explanation: This process covers how a teller issues a cashier's check at the window. Only account holders can get one, so the teller first confirms identity and checks that the person is an owner or authorized signer on the funding account. The teller then records the exact payee name, which is read back to the customer, plus the amount and remitter, who defaults to the account holder and cannot be someone else. Funds are checked against available balance, not ledger balance, and must cover the amount plus the $10 fee. If they don't, the customer can move money in from another account with the bank or lower the amount; the teller never overrides a shortfall. Premier accounts have the fee waived after the product code is verified. Anything over $10,000 needs a supervisor override in OCS before printing and a countersignature on the check. Once the account is debited and the check is printed on official stock, the customer checks the payee and amount before the teller signs. Any printing error after the check is printed gets voided, logged, and reprinted with a new serial number. The customer receives the check and receipt, and the bank copy goes in the end-of-day batch envelope.
trace_answers: A Premier Checking customer with enough available funds asking for a $12,500 cashier's check would have the fee waived after the product code is verified. Because the amount is over $10,000, a supervisor has to key in an override in OCS before the check will print. The account is debited $12,500, the check is printed from the locked drawer, the customer reviews the payee and amount, the teller signs, and the supervisor countersigns. The customer gets the check and receipt, and the bank copy goes in the batch envelope.

A standard checking customer asking for $4,000 with only $3,500 available is short of the $4,010 needed with the $10 fee. The teller asks about the savings account, and if the customer agrees, moves at least $510 from savings into checking and rechecks available balance. Once it covers $4,010, the $10 fee is charged, the account is debited $4,010, and the check is printed. No override is needed since the amount is under $10,000. The customer reviews it, the teller signs, and the check and receipt are handed over, with the bank copy going in the batch envelope.

answer.explanation: When someone reports a laptop lost or stolen, the process starts by logging a ticket and recording the user's account of the last sighting and whether the device was lost or taken, since that answer changes the steps later. The account is secured first by forcing a password reset and revoking all sessions and tokens, and the user is given a way to sign back in from another device. The laptop itself is then handled based on its encryption status: if it is encrypted with the key escrowed it gets a remote lock and a check-in is confirmed within 24 hours, otherwise it is wiped immediately and the Privacy Office is notified for a possible data exposure review. Stolen devices are held until a police report number is provided, and a manager reminder goes out after 5 business days without one. Once cleared, a replacement is requested from procurement and linked to the ticket, the asset is marked LOST or STOLEN, and the ticket is closed. If the device is recovered at any point, it must be reimaged at the service desk before returning to the network, the replacement is cancelled if not yet shipped, and the asset is returned to ACTIVE.
trace_answers: The laptop is treated as unencrypted, so the remote lock is skipped and a remote wipe is sent immediately. The Privacy Office is emailed with the ticket number and this is noted in the ticket. Because it was stolen, the ticket is put on hold until a police report number is received, and no replacement is ordered until then.

The lock was sent and the device did not check in within 24 hours, so a wipe is queued and noted. When the user finds the laptop two days later, they must not log back in; they bring it to the service desk to be reimaged before it goes back on the network. The replacement request is cancelled since it has not shipped, and the asset is set back to ACTIVE instead of LOST.

The traces are substantively correct, though trace 1 omits the 5-day manager reminder and trace 2 does not say the replacement was ordered because no police report was needed.

answer.explanation: This process handles requests for access to shared drive folders that come in through the portal. First the request is checked for a full folder path and a clear access level, and if either is missing it gets sent back to the user for the details. Once it's complete, the folder's owner is found in the Folder Owner Register and emailed for approval, and the ticket is set to Pending Approval. answer.explanation: A transfer credit file starts when transcripts arrive in the shared inbox and get logged in the tracker. Official status is checked first, and unofficial copies put the file on hold until an official copy comes in or the 30-day limit closes it out. Each course is then reviewed on its grade. Anything below C- is not transferable. Courses that count toward the declared major need a C or better, and a C- in one of those only earns general elective credit without a lookup. Other courses at C- or above are checked against the equivalency table, and a recent match is applied directly. Courses with no recent match go to the department faculty reviewer along with a syllabus, and the reviewer's decision is applied, with extra information requested when needed, up to two rounds. Silence for 10 business days goes to the department chair. Once every course has a result, all of it goes into degree audit, the total is capped at 64 credits by trimming electives, and the report goes to the student and advisor. New rulings are saved to the equivalency table with the date, but defaulted electives are left out since no one actually ruled on them. The tracker row is then closed as complete.

Wait up to 30 minutes for a sandbox verdict
If clean and headers pass, reply to the reporter thanking them, note FP in the ticket, and close it
Otherwise treat the email as malicious and search mail logs for every other recipient of the same message
Purge the message from all mailboxes using the admin console
Check web proxy logs for anyone who clicked a link or opened an attachment
If someone did, reset that user's password, isolate their laptop from the endpoint console, and page IT on-call
Send the reporter a short note confirming the email was malicious and removed
Add notes to the ticket and close it

branches: Yes: go to the clean-or-not check
No, sandbox hangs: treat the email as malicious and continue with the malicious steps

branches: Yes: false positive, reply to reporter thanking them, note FP, close ticket, skip the rest

answer.explanation: When an employee forwards a suspicious email to the phish-report mailbox, the process starts by opening a ticket within an hour that captures the sender, subject, and reporter. The full headers are pulled from the original message, and any links or attachments go to the sandbox. If the sandbox gives a clean result and the headers show SPF and DKIM passing from a known vendor or partner, the email is treated as a false positive, the reporter gets a thank-you reply, and the ticket is closed right away. Anything else, including a sandbox that does not answer within 30 minutes, is treated as malicious. In that case the team finds every other recipient in the mail logs, purges the message from all mailboxes, and checks the proxy logs for clicks or opens. Any user who interacted with it gets a password reset, a laptop isolation, and an IT on-call page. The reporter is told the email was confirmed and removed, and the ticket is closed with notes.
trace_answers: If the sandbox has no verdict after 30 minutes and the proxy logs show one employee clicked the link, the email is treated as malicious. The mail logs are searched for all other recipients, the message is purged from every mailbox through the admin console, and that employee's password is reset, their laptop is isolated from the endpoint console, and IT on-call is paged. The reporter gets a note saying the email was confirmed malicious and removed, and the ticket is closed with notes.

If the sandbox comes back clean and the headers pass SPF and DKIM from a known vendor, it is a false positive. The reporter gets a thank-you reply, the ticket gets an FP note, and the ticket is closed. None of the malicious steps run.

answer.explanation: Interns put their hours into the staff portal each week by Friday at 5pm. The portal pings their site supervisor, who checks the hours against the schedule. answer.explanation: When the lab system flags a critical result, the triage person grabs it and logs the time so the 60-minute clock is tracked from the lab flag time. They first confirm the patient using name and DOB, and if that doesn't line up they call the lab before going any further. Once it's confirmed they page the ordering provider and keep re-paging every 15 minutes, moving up to the on-call provider and then the medical director if nobody answers. When a provider calls back, the value gets read back and confirmed and that gets written in the result note. The provider then decides whether the patient goes straight to the ED, in which case the patient is called and the Riverside General ED charge nurse gets a handoff, or it's handled as a routine follow-up like a repeat lab with instructions and draw hours. The patient gets up to three call attempts over about an hour; if they still can't be reached, the provider decides on a welfare check or letter, and the alert stays open and goes to the next triage person. Only after the patient is reached and the call is documented does the alert get closed.

The patient answers on the first call, so they get told to go to the nearest ED and the Riverside General ED charge nurse gets a quick handoff with name, DOB, the value, and the ordering provider. Then the call gets documented in the patient record and the alert gets closed with the time.

b. The provider orders a repeat lab for tomorrow, but the patient can't be reached after three attempts. The provider gets told so they can decide whether to request a welfare check or send a letter. The alert doesn't get closed; it gets marked open, pt not reached in the critical log and handed off verbally to the next triage nurse. The repeat lab order and the draw hours don't really get given to the patient until someone actually reaches them.

answer.explanation: This process handles a lost or stolen company laptop from the first report through to closing the ticket. The first priority is locking the user out of their accounts by resetting the password and revoking sessions and tokens, so that whoever has the laptop cannot reach company email, VPN, or SSO. The user is then given a way to get back into their work from a loaner or phone. The device itself is handled based on its encryption status: encrypted devices with an escrowed key get a remote lock, while anything else is treated as exposed data, gets a remote wipe immediately, and triggers a notice to the Privacy Office. Stolen devices cannot be replaced until the user has filed a police report, which is required by insurance, and the ticket waits on hold until the report number comes in. After a replacement is requested and linked, the asset is marked LOST or STOLEN and the ticket is closed. If the device is found later, it must be reimaged at the service desk before going back on the network, even if it was only locked, and any replacement that has not shipped is cancelled and the asset returned to ACTIVE.
trace_answers: a. The device is treated as unencrypted, so the lock is skipped and a remote wipe is sent right away. The Privacy Office is emailed with the ticket number for a possible data-exposure review, and the ticket is noted that they were notified. Because the laptop was stolen, the ticket is put on hold until the user files a police report and sends the report number. No replacement is ordered until that number arrives, and if it does not come in after 5 business days, the user's manager is cc'd on a reminder while the ticket stays on hold.

b. The device was locked but did not check in within 24 hours, so a wipe is queued anyway and noted in the ticket. Since it was lost, no police report is needed, and the replacement request is submitted and linked to the ticket. When the device turns up two days later, the user has to bring it to the service desk to be reimaged before it goes back on the network, even though it was only locked. The replacement request is cancelly because it has not shipped, and the asset is set back to ACTIVE.

Determine where the secret leaked: public repo or internal-only repo
For a public leak, revoke or rotate the credential immediately and notify the owner without waiting for a reply
For an internal leak, notify the owner and give them 24 hours to rotate it themselves
If the owner does not rotate within 24 hours, SecOps rotates the credential
Create a history-rewrite subtask in the ticket for the owner to scrub the secret from repository history
If rotation breaks a production service, have the owner push the new key into their config or vault and keep the old key revoked
Pull access logs for the key from the commit timestamp through revocation and look for unfamiliar source IPs, regions, or user agents

branches: Yes: owner handles rotation and coordinates deploy
No response in 24 hours: SecOps rotates the credential

branches: Yes: do not restore old key; owner pushes new key into config or vault and old key stays dead
No: continue to log review

branches: Unrecognized sources or regions: escalate to Incident Response and leave ticket open and linked

answer.explanation: When a leaked secret alert comes in, the SecOps person first opens it and checks whether the string is real or just a placeholder or test fixture. Fake ones get closed as false positives. If the key is live, we look up who owns it in the secrets inventory, and if it is not there we dig through git history to find the person who committed it. The big split is whether the secret was in a public repo or an internal one. Public leaks get rotated right away since they have probably been scraped, and the owner gets pinged so they know something might break. Internal leaks go to the owner first with a 24 hour window to rotate it themselves, and if they do not respond we rotate it for them. After that the owner has to get the secret removed from git history and if a prod service broke they push the new key into their config or vault without bringing the old one back. Last step is pulling access logs from the commit time until revocation. If anything looks unfamiliar we hand it to Incident Response, otherwise we write it up and close it.
trace_answers: Because the key is in an internal-only repo and the owner never responded, SecOps would rotate it after the 24 hour window ends. The later log review showing calls from an unfamiliar region means it is unrecognized usage, so page Incident Response on-call, link the ticket, and leave the ticket open for them to take over.

The valid cloud key on a public repo gets rotated or revoked immediately without waiting for the owner. Then I ping the owner so they know their service may break. If production goes down, I do not restore the old key. The owner needs to push the new key into their config or vault, and the old key stays dead.

answer.explanation: Software requests come in through the portal and are first checked against the Approved Software List. answer.explanation: When a customer dies, the estate desk first needs a certified death certificate and the notifying person's government ID before doing anything to the accounts, otherwise only a soft flag goes on the profile. Once that is verified, every account the deceased owned gets a hard freeze and cards and automatic payments are cancelled the same day. Any federal benefit money deposited after the date of death is sent back to Treasury and that amount is held before anyone decides who gets the funds. Joint accounts with survivorship just get retitled to the surviving owner and the file is closed. For sole-owner accounts, a POD beneficiary can claim the money with ID, a death certificate copy and a supervisor sign-off without legal review. Without a POD, the balance after the hold decides whether a notarized small estate affidavit (under 25,000) or probate letters (25,000 or more) is needed, and the package goes to Legal Review. Rejections go back to the family to fix, and a second rejection goes to the Estate Services Manager. If the family goes silent for 90 days, the file goes to the Dormant Estate queue with the account still frozen. Approved payouts are issued as cashier's checks and then the accounts are closed with a closure letter and final interest statement.

The account stays frozen while that happens and is not paid out or closed by the desk.

The Social Security deposit after the date of death gets submitted to Treasury as a reclamation and that amount is held. The POD beneficiary then makes the claim with their ID and a copy of the death certificate, and the supervisor signs off with no legal review. The remaining balance goes out as a cashier's check to the beneficiary, and the held amount stays with Treasury.

answer.explanation: Refill requests come in through the patient portal or the refill phone line and get logged in the refill queue with the patient's details. The staff member then looks up the patient's record to see when they were last seen by their provider. If it was within the last year, the request goes to the nurse refill pool, where the RN checks the medication against the clinic protocol. Routine medications that meet protocol get approved and sent to the pharmacy by the RN, while controlled substances or anything off protocol get forwarded to the prescribing provider to approve or deny. If the last visit was more than a year ago, the request is not sent to nursing; the patient is called and asked to book a follow-up, and a single 30-day bridge supply can be authorized so they do not run out, which still goes through the nurse pool. Once the request is sent or denied, the patient gets a portal message or phone call with the result and the request is closed in the queue.
trace_answers: The request is not sent to the nurse pool for a normal refill. The patient is called and a follow-up appointment is booked. The blood pressure medication is not sent to the pharmacy at this point, so the patient would wait for the appointment.

The request goes to the nurse pool and the RN routes it to the prescribing provider's inbox because it is controlled. The provider is out for a week, so the request just sits in the inbox until the provider gets back and signs off.

answer.explanation: When a phishing report comes in, the first thing is to see whether the sender is on the vendor allowlist, since most reports turn out to be our own survey tool or payroll provider and can be closed fast. Anything not on the list goes into the sandbox, never opened on a regular machine. If the sandbox says it is just spam, a sender rule gets added and the ticket closes. If it is malicious, the team checks the mail logs for everyone else who got it, purges it from mailboxes, blocks the domain and URLs at the gateway, and asks every recipient whether they clicked or opened anything. Clicking leads to a password question: no password means a remote AV scan, and a typed password means a reset and session revocation. An opened attachment means isolating the device and escalating to SecOps as P1. Anyone who does not reply gets chased after 4 hours, and if they still do not answer by end of day, their proxy logs get checked to see whether they hit the bad URL. Finance or exec payment requests skip the normal queue and trigger immediate calls. Once everyone is accounted for, the awareness note goes out and the ticket gets closed.
trace_answers: Not allowlisted, sandbox malicious, 40 recipients: since 40 is over 25 it is a campaign, so page the SecOps on-call. Still purge the message from all mailboxes with the admin tool, block the sender domain and URLs at the gateway, and message every recipient. The one who clicked but gave no password gets a remote AV scan on their device, and that gets recorded in the ticket.

Recipient never replies: chase once by chat or phone after the 4-hour wait. If still nothing by end of day, check proxy logs for that user hitting the bad URL. If there is a hit, treat it as if they typed credentials and force a password reset and revoke sessions. If there is no hit, record no response, no proxy hit, and move on.

answer.explanation: This process handles MRI orders from the Imaging Auth queue and works out whether each one can be scheduled and under what authorization. The first step is checking eligibility. If the coverage is inactive or termed, the order goes to Financial Counseling for a self-pay estimate, and it either moves forward as self-pay or gets cancelled. If coverage is active, the team checks whether the payer requires auth for that MRI. When no auth is needed, the payer is called to confirm and the order goes to scheduling. When auth is needed, the team gathers the office note, imaging history, and conservative treatment records for spine cases, asks the provider for an addendum if the documents are thin, then submits through the payer portal and tracks the reference number. The request is checked daily until the payer approves, asks for more information, or denies it. Denials can lead to a peer-to-peer within 14 days, and if that fails, the provider chooses between an appeal and cancellation. Approved orders are scheduled within the auth window, and URGENT orders get scanned first with a retro auth submitted later.

answer.explanation: Requests come into the FW-Changes queue and are worked oldest first unless flagged as an emergency. Each one is checked for a complete form, with a blank expiry defaulting to 90 days, and any/any requests are rejected outright. External destinations get screened against the threat intel blocklist, and anything that hits is rejected and reported to the SOC. Everything else is scored on the risk sheet, with scores of 7 or above going to the security architect, who can approve, deny, or send it back for changes. Approved requests are implemented in the Tuesday or Thursday change window, unless it is a manager-approved emergency, which goes in right away with a retroactive CAB record. On the night the rule is staged, pushed, and tested with the requester; a passing test gets tagged with the ticket and expiry and the ticket is closed, while a failing test is rolled back, retried once, and then escalated if it fails again.

The ticket stays open and is not closed.

The emergency request is internal so it skips the blocklist check, and a score of 4 means no architect review; it gets implemented right away since the manager approved the tag. The test passes so I tag the rule with the ticket number and expiry date, notify the requester, and close the ticket. answer.explanation: Each incoming load request gets checked against the sales order first and then sorted into truckload or less-than-truckload based on pallet count and weight. Smaller loads are booked through the LTL rate portal with the cheapest approved carrier and go straight to scheduling the dock. Truckloads go to the routing guide for that lane, and carriers are tendered in ranking order with two hours to accept before a non-response counts as a reject. If the guide runs out, several approved brokers are asked for spot quotes and the lowest one is used if it is within 15 percent of contract, otherwise it needs sign-off from the logistics manager or the on-call transportation director after 4pm. If approval is refused, the load goes back to the order desk to push the ship date and comes back into the queue. Once a carrier is locked in, the pickup is scheduled, paperwork goes to the carrier, and the sales order is updated with the carrier and PRO number so customer service can track it. On pickup day the dock board is monitored, and a no-show beyond two hours or a cancellation triggers a re-tender down the list, and after pickup the carrier results are recorded for procurement.

The primary carrier does not respond within 2 hours, which counts as a reject, and the only backup also rejects, so the guide is exhausted and approved brokers are emailed for spot quotes. The lowest quote at 5pm is 22 percent over contract, which is outside the 15 percent limit and after the 4pm cutoff, so it goes to the on-call transportation director. If approved, the load is awarded and the carrier is locked in; if not approved, the load goes back to the order desk to renegotiate the ship date and returns through the queue as a new request, and it is not held overnight.

The carrier accepted the tender but the driver has not shown up 2.5 hours after the appointment, which is past the 2-hour window and counts as a bounce. The bounce is marked on that carrier's scorecard, the load is re-tendered starting with the next carrier in the routing guide after the one that bounced (or to spot if no carriers are left), and the dock appointment is rebooked for the new carrier.

answer.explanation: This process handles impossible travel sign-in alerts by first ruling out expected causes like corporate VPN exits or approved travel, then checking with the account owner directly. answer.explanation: This process handles tuition reimbursement from the first request through final payment. An employee sends a TR-1 pre-approval form before the course starts. If the start date has already passed, the request goes to the HR Director, who decides whether to make an exception; without an exception, the employee receives a late-submission decline. Requests that move forward are checked in the HRIS for at least six months of tenure and no current PIP. Anyone failing that check gets a not-eligible decline and the request is closed as ineligible. Eligible requests go to the direct manager for job-relatedness approval. A decline from the manager is passed on to the employee and closes the request. An approval activates the request in the tracker and triggers the approval letter, which explains the annual cap and the deadline for submitting grades and receipts. If the manager does not respond, one reminder goes out after five business days, and if there is still no answer three business days later, the manager's director decides. After the course, the employee submits the grade report and itemized receipt. A grade below B (Pass is accepted for pass/fail courses) ends the process with no payment. Otherwise, the eligible tuition and required fees are reimbursed up to whatever remains of the $5,250 calendar-year cap after YTD payments. The amount goes to payroll by Wednesday for the next cycle, and once payroll confirms, the employee is told the amount and pay date and the request is closed as paid with YTD updated.

answer.explanation: This process starts when QC flags a bad lot and the lot is placed on QC HOLD in the WMS. Once the hold is confirmed, the team pulls the original PO and supplier agreement to get the line, lot, quantity, and unit cost, then emails the supplier rep for an RMA with the RTV template and QC's defect report and photos attached. answer.explanation: When someone reports a suspicious email, the first thing I do is check whether the sender is on our vendor allowlist, since most reports turn out to be our own HR survey tool or the payroll provider and can be closed right away. Anything not on the list goes to the sandbox, never onto my own machine. If the sandbox says it is just junk, I add a spam rule and close it. If it is malicious or suspicious, I search the mail logs for everyone else who got the same subject and sender, and if it is more than 25 people I page SecOps on-call, though I still purge and block myself without waiting. The purge uses the admin tool, with shared mailboxes handled by asking the owner's admin to delete manually and recording who I asked. The sender domain and URLs get blocked at the gateway, then every recipient gets asked whether they clicked anything. I give people four hours, chase once, and if there is still nothing by end of day I check proxy logs. Each person's answer determines the follow-up: nothing touched means no action, a clicked link means either a remote AV scan or a password reset and session revoke depending on whether they typed credentials, and an opened attachment means isolating the device and escalating as P1 without trying to clean it. Once everyone is accounted for, I post a short awareness note with blurred links and close the ticket after updating it.
trace_answers: 4a: Since the sender is not allowlisted and the sandbox says malicious, I search the mail logs and find 40 recipients, which is over 25, so I page the SecOps on-call as a campaign. For the one who clicked the link but did not type a password, I kick off a remote AV scan on their device and record it, and no password reset or session revoke is needed.

4b: If a recipient never replies to the did-you-click message, I wait four hours, then chase once by chat or phone. If there is still no reply by end of day, I check the proxy logs for that user hitting the bad URL. If there is a proxy hit, I treat it as if they entered credentials, so I force a password reset and revoke all their active sessions. If there is no proxy hit, I record no response and no proxy hit and move on. The process does not say what to do if not everyone ends up accounted for, so I would need to ask about that case.

answer.explanation: This process covers the weekly replenishment of inventory that has fallen to or below its reorder point. Each Monday the Below ROP report is pulled, and before any order is placed the open POs are checked so the same gap is not ordered twice. Uncovered SKUs get a PO built from the approved vendor list at the listed price, with a need date based on lead time or flagged as ASAP if stock is already zero. After the PO is sent, the supplier is expected to confirm a ship date within two business days, with follow-up emails and a phone call if they do not. If the supplier still gives no firm date, the order is cancelled and moved to the backup supplier. The confirmed date is compared to the need date, with expedite requests and shortage tracking used when it falls more than five business days late. answer.explanation: Each morning before the first wave, the day's cycle count list is pulled from the WMS, which selects about 40 bins weighted by ABC class. Every bin on that list gets a count hold so pickers cannot take product from it during the count. Counts are done blind, meaning the expected quantity is hidden from the counter, and quantities are keyed in eaches. The system checks each count against on-hand and only lets the adjustment post automatically if the difference is under 2 percent and under $50. Anything outside that range gets a blind recount by someone other than the original counter, and the two counts plus the system quantity determine whether the first count was a mistake or a real variance. A real variance triggers research into open picks, unconfirmed putaways, unput-away receipts, and neighboring bins, since product is often slotted one bin over. If the cause is found, the transaction is corrected instead of adjusting inventory. If not, an adjustment request goes to the shift supervisor for approval. Every bin that goes out of tolerance is logged in the shared tracker, and holds that run too long during a wave can be ended early by the supervisor, sending that bin back to the next day's list.
trace_answers: The first count is confirmed as a real variance because the recount matched it, so research starts. The unconfirmed putaway is found as the cause, so the putaway gets confirmed in the WMS with no inventory adjustment needed. The hold is then released and the bin is logged in the tracker with the cause code for an unconfirmed putaway.

The recount matches neither the first count nor the system, so Dana does a third count. Dana's count matches the first count, so it is treated as the recount and the variance is treated as real. Research finds no cause, so an adjustment request goes to the shift supervisor for sign-off. Once approved and posted, the hold is released and the bin is logged as unexplained.

Both trace answers match the key, and nothing added contradicts or goes beyond the workflow.

After a wipe is sent, the desk keeps checking for confirmation and resends every 4 hours, and after 72 hours without confirmation it goes to Security and the asset is marked as an unconfirmed wipe. answer.explanation: This process handles reported phishing emails from intake to closure. Reports arrive either through the mail client button, which creates a ticket with the original message attached, or as forwarded emails, which need to be re-sent as attachments so the headers survive. The first check is whether the sender is on the approved vendor list, since many reports are legitimate internal or vendor mail and can be closed quickly. Anything else goes to a sandbox so nobody has to open suspicious links on a normal machine. Harmless junk gets a sender spam rule and a reply. Malicious or suspicious messages trigger a broader response: the mail logs are searched for everyone else who received it, the message is purged from mailboxes, and the sender domain and URLs are blocked at the gateway. Every recipient is then asked whether they interacted with it, and their answer determines whether a device scan, a password reset with session revocation, or a device isolation with SecOps escalation is needed. If people don't respond, the process allows four hours, one follow-up, and then a proxy log check at end of day to decide whether to treat them as compromised. Finance or executive requests for payments or bank changes skip the queue and bring in Security Ops and the Finance manager right away. The process ends with a short staff awareness post and a complete ticket update.
trace_answers: Because the sender is not allowlisted and the sandbox returned malicious, the full malicious path applies: the mail logs are searched and since 40 recipients exceeds 25, the SecOps on-call is paged, while the purge and gateway blocks of the sender domain and URLs are done immediately without waiting. The message is purged from all mailboxes, shared mailbox failures get a manual deletion request to the owner's admin recorded in the ticket, and every recipient gets the click question. The person who clicked the link but did not type a password gets a remote AV scan on their device, which is recorded in the ticket, with no password reset.

If the recipient never replies, they get the four-hour window, then one chase by chat or phone. If there is still no answer by end of day, the proxy logs are checked for that user hitting the bad URL. A proxy hit means the user is treated as having entered credentials, so their password is reset and all active sessions are revoked. No proxy hit means the ticket records 'no response, no proxy hit' and the process moves on without further action.

answer.explanation: When a mailbox full ticket comes in, I log it under Email > Quota and make sure the user's name, department and email are on it, double checking the email in case it came from a personal phone. Then I pull up the mailbox in the admin console, compare usage to the 50 GB cap, and screenshot the usage panel to attach. If the user is under 90%, it is mostly people seeing the approaching limit warning, so I send the KB-0412 cleanup guide and resolve it. If they are at 90% or more, I contact them and set up a 15 minute remote session to turn on online archive, which moves mail older than 2 years out of the main mailbox. answer.explanation: This process handles firewall change requests that come into a shared queue, oldest first unless a request is flagged as an emergency. Each request first has its form checked for the required fields, and if something is missing it goes back to the requester and waits up to five business days before being auto-abandoned. A blank expiry date is not a reason to reject; it just gets set to 90 days. Any request that opens every source or every port is rejected straight away. External destinations get checked against the threat intel blocklist, and anything on it is rejected and reported to the SOC. Everything else is scored on the risk sheet. Low scores can be approved directly, while scores of 7 or more go to the security architect, who can approve, deny, or send it back for changes. Approved requests are put in the next Tuesday or Thursday change window, unless they are manager-approved emergencies, which go in right away. On the night the rule is staged, pushed, and tested with the requester. A passing test means the rule gets tagged with the ticket number and expiry, and the ticket is closed. A failing test means rolling back, working with the network team, and retrying once; if that also fails, the ticket is marked Failed Implementation and escalated instead of closed. Emergency changes also need a retroactive CAB record within 24 hours, and if CAB rejects it the rule is removed.

On the change night the rule is staged, pushed, and tested with the requester. The first test fails, so it is rolled back right away and the network team is asked what went wrong. After the fix, the retry also fails, so it is rolled back again, the ticket is marked Failed Implementation, escalated to the network eng lead, and the requester is told it has been escalated. The ticket is left open and not closed.

The request is an emergency with manager approval and an internal destination, so the blocklist check is skipped and it is scored at 4, which means it is approved directly without the architect. It skips the change window and is implemented right away. The connectivity test passes, so the rule is tagged with the ticket number and expiry, the requester is notified, and the ticket is closed. A retroactive CAB record is filed within 24 hours. Because CAB rejects it, the rule is pulled from the policy manager.

answer.explanation: When a leaked secret alert comes in, the SecOps person first opens it and checks whether the key or token is actually valid, since a lot of them are test data or placeholders, and closes it as a false positive if it is dead. For live secrets, the next step is finding out who owns it from the secrets inventory, and if it is not listed you dig through git blame to find the committer. Where the leak happened decides the urgency: a public repo means rotating right away and telling the owner afterward, while an internal repo gives the owner a day to rotate it themselves before SecOps does it. After rotation the owner has to scrub the secret out of repo history and assign that subtask to them. If the rotation breaks something in production, the old key stays dead and the owner loads the new one into their config or vault. Finally the access logs get pulled from the commit time up to revocation, and anything that does not match the owning service gets handed to Incident Response while the SecOps ticket stays linked, otherwise the case is written up and closed.
trace_answers: The secret is live in an internal-only repo so the owner gets 24 hours to rotate it, and since they never respond SecOps rotates it after that window, then the history rewrite request goes to the owner in the ticket and the prod check is done. When the log review shows calls from an unfamiliar region, the on-call Incident Response person gets paged, the ticket is linked to them, and IR takes ownership while the SecOps ticket stays open and linked.

A valid cloud key on a public repo gets revoked and rotated right away without waiting on the owner, and the owner is pinged that their service may break. Since rotation takes down production, the old key is not restored and the owner has to push the new key into their config or vault, and the old key stays dead. After that the access logs are pulled from the commit time to revocation and reviewed, and the history rewrite request is assigned to the owner.

Every recipient then gets asked whether they clicked, and the follow-up depends on whether they clicked a link, typed a password, or opened an attachment. Non-responders get one chase, then a proxy log check at end of day that decides whether they are treated as if they gave up credentials. stages: Family member calls or walks in; record the date of death and the relationship to the deceased

Require a certified death certificate (raised seal or state e-certificate) and government ID from the person notifying us before any freeze; if only an obituary or a phone call is available, place a soft reported-deceased flag on the profile
Place a hard freeze on every account where the deceased is an owner, cancel debit and credit cards, and stop autopays and scheduled transfers the same day
Pull transaction history from the date of death forward and submit a reclamation to Treasury for any Social Security, VA, or other federal benefit deposits received after death, holding that amount
Determine the ownership type of each account
For joint accounts with right of survivorship: remove the deceased from title, retitle to the survivor, lift the freeze for the survivor, and close the file without legal review
For sole-owner accounts: check the account record for a POD beneficiary
If a POD beneficiary exists: beneficiary provides their own ID and a copy of the death certificate, and a branch operations supervisor signs the claim form

If no POD beneficiary exists: determine the balance after the reclamation hold and collect either a notarized small estate affidavit (under $25,000) or letters testamentary or letters of administration from probate court naming the executor ($25,000 or more)
Send the package to Legal Review (internal queue, about 5 business days)
If Legal Review rejects the package: send the requester the rejection reasons so they can correct and resubmit, which returns the file to Legal Review
If Legal Review rejects the same file a second time: stop the back-and-forth and escalate to the Estate Services Manager
If requested documents are not received within 90 days: keep the account frozen and move the file to the Dormant Estate queue without closing it

On approval (supervisor sign-off for POD, legal approval for estate): issue a cashier's check payable to the beneficiary or to the estate in the executor's name as representative, close the account(s), and mail the closure letter with the final interest statement

answer.explanation: When a family member reports a customer has died, the first job is to get the date of death and the relationship, then hold off on any freeze until a certified death certificate and the notifying person's government ID are in hand; a phone call or obituary only gets a soft flag. Once documents are verified, the account is hard frozen and cards and automatic payments are stopped the same day. Next, we check for federal benefit payments that came in after the date of death and send those back to Treasury while holding the amount, before deciding who gets the money. Joint accounts with survivorship simply move to the survivor and stop there. Sole-owner accounts are checked for a POD beneficiary, who can be paid after an ID check, a copy of the death certificate, and a supervisor's signature. Without a POD, the balance after the hold decides whether a notarized small estate affidavit or probate letters are needed, and the file goes to Legal Review. Rejected files go back to the family to fix, but a second rejection goes up to the Estate Services Manager. If the family goes silent for 90 days, the file moves to the Dormant Estate queue and stays frozen. Approved money is paid by cashier's check to the beneficiary or to the estate in the executor's name, and then the accounts are closed with a closure letter and final interest statement.

answer.explanation: When a customer asks for a replacement debit card, the teller first makes sure the person is the account holder by checking a government photo ID and the last four digits of their SSN. If the ID does not match, the teller stops, does not talk about the account, and sends the person to the branch manager. Once identity is confirmed, the teller asks why the card is needed. If CardDesk errors out, which tends to happen in the morning, the teller waits a few minutes and tries again; after three failures a paper Card Request Form goes into the ops tray for entry by end of day and the customer gets a copy of that form. answer.explanation: When an impossible travel alert comes in, I pull the username, both IPs, their geo and the timestamps into the ticket first. Then I check whether the IPs are on the egress list or whether HR has an approved travel entry for that exact country, since a travel entry for a different country doesn't count. If neither applies, I check the Privileged group. Privileged accounts get locked down right away and the IR lead gets pinged, and I reach out to the user after. For everyone else I message the user on Teams or by phone, not email, and ask if both sign-ins were them. If they confirm, it's closed as benign with a note on what they said. answer.explanation: When a refill request comes in by portal or phone, whoever picks it up logs it in the refill queue and looks at the patient's record to see when they were last seen. If that visit was within the last year, the request goes to the nurse pool, where an RN checks the medication against the refill protocol. Routine medications that are on protocol get approved and sent to the pharmacy right away. Controlled substances or anything off protocol get passed to the prescribing provider, who either approves and sends the prescription or denies it. If the patient was last seen more than a year ago, the request does not go to nursing; instead the patient is called and booked for a follow-up, and the clinic can give one 30-day bridge supply that still goes through the nurse pool. Once the request is sent or denied, the patient gets told the outcome and the request gets closed. Provider inbox items are supposed to be handled within two business days, and if one sits longer than that, the RN escalates it to whichever provider is covering that day.

The RN checks it against the protocol, sees that it is a routine on-protocol medication, approves it, and e-sends it to the pharmacy. Then the patient is told the outcome by portal message or phone and the request is closed.

b. Because the last visit was 3 months ago, the request goes to the nurse pool. Since it is a controlled substance, the RN routes it to the prescribing provider's inbox instead of approving it directly. The provider is out for a week, so the item sits there. Once it has been sitting for 2 business days, the RN escalates it to the covering provider for that day. The covering provider approves or denies it. If approved, it is e-sent to the pharmacy. Either way, the patient is notified of the outcome and the request is closed.

answer.explanation: This process makes sure every patient discharged from Lakeside Regional to one of our PCPs gets a follow-up call within two business days. Each morning the discharge list is pulled from the Transitions report, which catches observation stays that the ADT screen misses, and the names are split evenly among staff and added to the shared TCM queue under each person's initials. Before calling, the caller reads the discharge summary to pick up the diagnosis, new medications, and any follow-up the hospital already ordered, since that is what helps catch medication problems later. If the patient has been readmitted, the task is closed as readmitted and no call is made. On the call, identity is verified with name and date of birth; if someone else answers, they can only be spoken with if they are an authorized contact, otherwise the caller just asks for a callback and discusses nothing. Missed calls get a generic voicemail and are retried the next business day up to three times, after which a letter goes out and the PCP is told the patient was never reached. Wrong or disconnected numbers skip the retries and go straight to the letter, PCP message, and a registration ticket. Once the patient is reached, a symptom screen is run. Emergency symptoms like chest pain, trouble breathing, confusion, or fainting send the patient to 911 and the PCP gets an urgent message; other red flags trigger a warm transfer to the triage nurse line, and the caller comes back later that day to finish the medication reconciliation and appointment. Medication mismatches trigger a pharmacist review message without holding up the call. The appointment step confirms an existing PCP visit within seven days, schedules one if the PCP has an opening, or books with the care team NP if not. The call is then documented in the TCM template and the task is closed.
trace_answers: If the spouse answers and is not an authorized contact, the caller asks for a callback at the clinic number, discusses nothing, and logs that as the first no-contact attempt. The next two calls go unanswered, so each gets a generic voicemail and is logged as an attempt, which brings the total to three. After the third miss, the outreach letter is mailed and the PCP gets a staff message saying the patient was not reached, and the task is closed.

A fever of 102 is a red flag but not in the 911 group, so the caller does a warm transfer to the triage nurse line while the patient is still on the phone. Later that day the caller goes back to the patient to finish med rec and appointment. The patient still taking a stopped medication is a mismatch, so a pharmacist review message goes out and the call continues without waiting for pharmacy. With no PCP openings within seven days, the visit is booked with the NP on the care team, and then the call is documented in the TCM template and the task is closed.

answer.explanation: This process takes a load request from the Outbound Loads queue, checks the pallet count, weight, and ship date against the sales order since the order desk often gets the summary wrong, and then decides between LTL and FTL based on the 12 pallet or 15,000 lb threshold. LTL loads get booked through the LTL rate portal with the cheapest approved carrier and go straight to the dock. FTL loads go to the routing guide for that lane, where each ranked carrier gets a 2 hour window to accept in TMS, and a silent carrier counts as a reject so the team keeps moving down the list. If every carrier in the guide fails, the team asks at least three approved brokers for spot quotes and takes the lowest one; if it is within 15% of contract it can be awarded right away, otherwise it needs logistics manager approval before 4pm or the on-call transportation director after 4pm, and a denial sends the load back to the order desk to renegotiate the ship date. Once a carrier is locked in, the pickup appointment is booked with the dock scheduler, the BOL and load details go to the carrier, and the sales order gets the carrier name and PRO number for customer service tracking. On pickup day, a driver more than 2 hours late is a bounce that gets marked on the scorecard, and the load is re-tendered to the next carrier down the guide or to spot, and the dock is rebooked. A carrier that cancels before pickup is handled the same way as a reject, and after pickup the tender results for each carrier are logged on the scorecard sheet for the quarterly procurement bid.
trace_answers: The primary carrier gets 2 hours to respond and since there is no response it counts as a reject, so the load goes to the only backup carrier, who also rejects. That leaves the guide with no carriers, so the load goes to spot. At least 3 approved brokers get emailed for quotes and the lowest one comes in at 22% over contract. Since it is 5pm, after the 4pm cutoff, the approval request goes to the on-call transportation director instead of the logistics manager. If the director approves, the load gets awarded at that rate and then booked with the dock. If the director says no, the load goes back to the order desk so the customer can push the ship date, and it comes back through the queue as a new request.

The primary carrier accepted the tender, so it is locked in and the pickup appointment is already booked. The driver is 2.5 hours late, which is past the 2 hour window, so it counts as a bounce. That bounce gets marked on the primary carrier's scorecard. The load is then re-tendered starting with the next carrier in the guide after the primary, or spot if there are no carriers left, and the dock appointment gets rebooked for the new carrier.
